decisions.reason: Nordahl and Wells (2018) conduct a preliminary evaluation of generic Metacognitive Therapy (MCT; Wells, 2009) for Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) across three patients of increasing clinical complexity using an A–B single-case design. The term 'Replication Series' in the title and 'systematic replication (Barlow and Hersen, 1984)' in the Introduction and Materials and Methods refer to within-study single-case replication across the three patients to establish generalizability across SAD subtypes. The shipped original study, Wells and Papageorgiou (2001) (a brief cognitive therapy case series based on Clark and Wells's 1995 cognitive model), is cited only once in the entire paper (Introduction, alongside Nordahl et al., 2016b) as background contrast: the authors explain that those earlier abbreviated treatments relied on the CBT model, included testing negative thoughts, and omitted core MCT components, whereas generic MCT 'has yet to be evaluated in its purer form in SAD.' Wells and Papageorgiou (2001) is never mentioned or compared in the Methods, Results, or Discussion. Under the Codebook, evaluating a distinct, previously untested pure-MCT intervention protocol with internal across-case repetition is not_a_replication.

previous_decisions.quote: In accordance with Wells’ (2000) metacognitive therapy approach, two studies (Wells and Papageorgiou, 2001; Nordahl et al., 2016b) have shown that a briefer and more metacognitive focused intervention can be highly effective and time efficient. However, these studies left out several important components which are emphasised in the metacognitive model (Wells and Matthews, 1994, 1996) and retained some of the cognitive components of the Clark and Wells (1995) treatment.
previous_decisions.reason: Because the study is not a replication of a previously published finding, the original study field is inapplicable; Wells and Papageorgiou (2001) is cited only as background contrast to motivate testing a purer form of MCT.

previous_decisions.quote: The present study aimed to explore the effects of generic MCT for SAD. Treatment related effects were evaluated using direct replication single case (A–B) methodology across three patients with different subtypes of SAD; performance type, generalised and generalised plus avoidant personality disorder, representing increasing SAD severity/complexity. All patients responded during treatment and achieved substantial symptom reductions which were largely maintained at 6 months’ follow-up.
previous_decisions.reason: Because the study is an original single-case series rather than a replication of a prior published study, a replication outcome is inapplicable; the shipped quote describes primary clinical treatment response across the three cases.
